question: Which statement best describes What .d.ts files are?
options: Ambient declarations describe things that exist globally or come from non-code imports. declare global { interface Window { myFlag: boolean } } adds to the global scope; declare module '*.svg' types asset imports. They live in .d.ts files included by the project and require no import to take effect.

declare introduces an ambient declaration: it tells the compiler 'this thing exists at runtime, trust me' without generating code. Use it for globals (declare const VERSION: string), module shapes, or to describe APIs provided by the environment. It is the core building block of every declaration file.

A .d.ts file contains only type information — no runtime code is emitted from it. It describes the shape of values that exist elsewhere (a JS library, a global, your own compiled output). The compiler emits .d.ts for your own library so consumers get types; you also write them by hand to type code that has none.

DefinitelyTyped is a community repo of .d.ts files for thousands of untyped packages, published under the @types scope (e.g. npm i -D @types/lodash). TypeScript auto-discovers @types packages, so installing one is usually all you need to get full typings for an otherwise untyped library.

Module augmentation extends an existing module's types from your own code: open the module with declare module 'name' and add new members (e.g. a plugin adds a method to express's Request, or a field to a library interface). It merges with the original declarations instead of replacing them.

When a package has no types and no @types entry, you write a small .d.ts: declare module 'pkg-name' and export the functions/values you use with your best-guess types. Start narrow (just what you call), tighten over time, and prefer unknown over any so unsafe usage is still flagged.
